posts.title: Why we train in groups of six
posts.excerpt: Six is the most people one coach can truly watch. Here is how we arrived at the number, and why we will not change it.
posts.content:
When we opened, classes had ten places. Within a month we had cut them to six.

What a coach can see

A coach watching a squat is looking at feet, knees, hips, spine and breath at once. With six people, each one gets a proper look every set. With ten, somebody is always missed.

What it costs

Fewer places means fuller classes and a slightly higher price. We think that is the right trade: nobody gets stronger by being overlooked.

posts.title: The kettlebell swing, taught slowly
posts.excerpt: The swing looks simple and is easy to get wrong. We teach it in three weeks, not three minutes.
posts.content:
The swing is a hinge, not a squat, and not a front raise. Most of our first week is spent without a bell at all.

Week one: the hinge

Hands on hips, push them back to the wall, stand tall. Repeat until it is boring.

Week two: the hike

A light bell, hiked back between the legs and set down again. No swing yet.

Week three: the swing

Only now do we let it float. It usually looks good on the first try, because the parts were already there.

posts.title: Sleep is the session you skip
posts.excerpt: You do not get stronger in the studio. You get stronger in the eight hours afterwards, if you let yourself.
posts.content:
Training is the signal; recovery is where the change happens. Of everything we track in the logbooks, sleep predicts a good session best.

Three small habits

The same bedtime, a darker room, and no heavy training after nine in the evening. None of it is new, all of it works.

posts.title: Ten minutes of mobility before the desk
posts.excerpt: A short routine from Mio for the mornings when you cannot come in: hips, spine and shoulders, in ten quiet minutes.
posts.content:
This is the first ten minutes of our Wednesday class, adapted for a living room floor.

The routine

Two minutes of slow breathing on your back. Two minutes of hip circles on hands and knees. Three minutes of side bends, seated. Three minutes of shoulder rolls against a wall.

Do it daily for a month and tell us what changed.

posts.title: Rowing intervals that leave room for tomorrow
posts.excerpt: Conditioning should make you fitter, not flatten you. How we plan our Tuesday intervals.
posts.content:
A hard rowing session is easy to design and hard to recover from. Ours are planned to finish with something left.

The shape

Eight rounds of one minute steady and one minute easy, with the steady pace set by your breath, not your ego. When you can talk in short sentences, the pace is right.

posts.title: Chalk, grip and the first pull-up
posts.excerpt: Most first pull-ups arrive between week ten and week sixteen. What we do in the weeks before.
posts.content:
The pull-up is the lift members ask about most. It is also the one that rewards patience most clearly.

Hang first

Every class ends with a dead hang. Ten seconds becomes thirty, thirty becomes a minute. Grip comes first.

Then lower slowly

Jump to the top, lower over five seconds. When five of those feel calm, the first full pull-up is usually close.
